meta.titre: Folds, Faults and Unconformities: reading deformed rock sequences and measuring displacement

sections.contenu_markdown: A road cutting beside a highway in Cameroon can show layered rocks bent into an arch, a straight crack that cuts through them, and flat layers lying on top of tilted ones. Each feature records a different episode in the history of the rocks. Engineers planning a road, a tunnel or a dam, and mining companies planning a shaft, must locate such structures, because a fault zone can leak water or collapse and folding decides where a seam of ore or coal will be found. At the GCE this topic appears as outcrop patterns, definitions such as throw and heave, classifications of faults and the order of events in a cross-section.

items: Sedimentary rocks are laid down in layers called beds, and in an undisturbed sequence the oldest bed is at the bottom.
Dip is the angle at which a bed or a fault plane slopes below the horizontal, and strike is the direction of a horizontal line on that surface.
Compression squeezes rock together and tension pulls it apart.
Sine and tangent of an angle relate the sides of a right-angled triangle.

sections.titre: Folds, faults and unconformities: vocabulary, classification and displacement
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Folds
A **fold** is a bend in originally flat rock layers, produced mainly by compression. The **limbs** are the two sides, the **hinge** is the line of greatest curvature, and the **axial plane** divides the fold into two roughly equal halves.
- **Anticline**: arch-shaped; in an undisturbed sequence the oldest beds lie in the core and the limbs dip away from the axis.
- **Syncline**: trough-shaped; the youngest beds lie in the core and the limbs dip towards the axis.

Folds are also described as symmetrical, asymmetrical, overturned (one limb tilted past the vertical), recumbent (axial plane near horizontal) or isoclinal (limbs parallel), and as gentle, open, close or tight. A fold whose hinge is tilted **plunges**; its outcrop makes a V-shaped closure.

### Faults
A **fault** is a fracture along which the blocks on either side have moved. The block above an inclined fault plane is the **hanging wall** and the block below is the **footwall**. **Throw** is the vertical displacement and **heave** the horizontal displacement, both measured in a vertical section at right angles to the strike of the fault. For a dip-slip fault that displaces a horizontal bed, with fault dip $\delta$:

$$\tan\delta = \frac{\text{throw}}{\text{heave}} \qquad \text{net slip} = \frac{\text{throw}}{\sin\delta}$$

| Fault | Dip | Movement | Stress |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | usually steep | hanging wall moves down | tension |
| Reverse | above about $45^\circ$ | hanging wall moves up | compression |
| Thrust | below about $45^\circ$ | hanging wall moves up and over | strong compression |
| Strike-slip | near vertical | blocks slide sideways (sinistral or dextral) | shear |
| Oblique-slip | any | vertical and sideways together | combined |

Evidence of faulting includes displaced beds, polished grooved surfaces (slickensides), broken rock (fault breccia) and fine crushed rock (gouge). A vertical borehole that crosses a normal fault omits beds, while one that crosses a reverse fault repeats them. Paired normal faults make a down-dropped **graben** (rift valley) beside a raised **horst**.

### Unconformities
An **unconformity** is an erosion surface (or a surface of non-deposition) that separates younger rocks from older rocks and represents a gap in time.

| Type | Description |
|---|---|
| Angular | older beds tilted or folded and eroded, younger beds above at a different angle |
| Disconformity | beds parallel above and below an uneven erosion surface |
| Nonconformity | sedimentary rocks lying on eroded igneous or metamorphic rock |

Evidence: a basal conglomerate containing pebbles of the rock below, a weathered zone, truncated structures, and a break in the fossil record.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks you to define, distinguish between terms, or outline a classification.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give a precise definition of each term and add the contrast in the same sentence (for example, throw is vertical while heave is horizontal). For a classification, say what the basis is (dip, relative movement, stress) and give one feature for each class. Each correct and distinct point earns a mark, so a short table is efficient.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When dip, throw, heave or a drawn section is given.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Draw a right-angled triangle with throw vertical, heave horizontal and the fault plane as the sloping side, and check that the angle used is the dip of the fault, not the dip of a bed. For a section, name each structure, then list events from oldest to youngest using cross-cutting relationships: a fault or an intrusion is younger than everything it cuts and older than anything that lies across it undisturbed.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question describes the age pattern of rocks at the surface after erosion.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Read the ages from the centre outwards. Oldest rocks in the centre with younger rocks outwards means an anticline; youngest in the centre means a syncline. The pattern is mirrored across the axial plane. In a plunging anticline the V of the outcrop points in the direction of plunge, and in a plunging syncline the V opens in that direction.

sections.enonce_markdown: A cliff shows horizontal beds of sandstone, shale and coal cut by a straight fault that dips at $60^\circ$. The hanging wall has moved down, and a coal seam is displaced vertically by $30\ \mathrm{m}$. The beds are eroded to a level surface. On it lies a conglomerate containing pebbles of the sandstone, followed by horizontal limestone. The conglomerate and the limestone are not displaced by the fault. (a) Name the fault and the stress that formed it. (b) Calculate the heave and the net slip. (c) Name the type of unconformity and give two pieces of evidence. (d) Give the order of events.

etapes.action: Classify the fault from the movement of the hanging wall.
etapes.justification: A fault whose hanging wall has moved down relative to the footwall is a normal fault, and normal faults form when the crust is stretched.
Throw and heave are the sides of a right-angled triangle with the fault plane as the sloping side, so $\tan\delta = \text{throw}/\text{heave}$.
Net slip is the displacement along the fault plane, the sloping side of the triangle: $\text{throw}/\sin\delta$.
The beds are parallel on both sides of the erosion surface, so there is no angular difference; this is a disconformity.
etapes.resultat_markdown: **Disconformity**. Evidence: a basal conglomerate with pebbles of the sandstone below, and the fault stops at the erosion surface.

etapes.justification: A fault is older than the rocks that lie across it without being displaced, and each bed is younger than the one it rests on.
etapes.resultat_markdown: (1) Deposition of sandstone, shale and coal; (2) faulting; (3) erosion to a level surface; (4) deposition of conglomerate and limestone.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The fault is a normal fault formed by tension, with a heave of $17.3\ \mathrm{m}$ and a net slip of $34.6\ \mathrm{m}$. The junction below the limestone is a disconformity, and the unbroken limestone shows that faulting came before the final deposition.

items.erreur_markdown: "Throw is the distance the blocks moved along the fault and heave is the width of the fault zone."
items.pourquoi_faux: Throw and heave are the vertical and horizontal components of the displacement. The distance moved along the plane is the net slip.
items.correction_markdown: Throw is the vertical displacement and heave the horizontal displacement; for a horizontal bed, net slip $= \sqrt{\text{throw}^2 + \text{heave}^2}$.

items.erreur_markdown: "An anticline is a hill and a syncline is a valley."
items.pourquoi_faux: Anticline and syncline describe the arrangement of the beds, not the shape of the land. Erosion often removes the crest of an anticline and leaves a valley.
items.correction_markdown: Use the ages on the map: oldest rocks in the core means an anticline, youngest in the core means a syncline.

items.erreur_markdown: "The hanging wall of a normal fault is the block that moved up."
items.pourquoi_faux: Hanging wall and footwall are defined by position (above and below the fault plane), not by the direction of movement. In a normal fault the hanging wall moves down.
items.correction_markdown: Locate the hanging wall first, then say whether it moved down (normal) or up (reverse).

items.erreur_markdown: "A reverse fault forms when the crust is pulled apart by tension."
items.pourquoi_faux: Tension stretches the crust and produces normal faults. A reverse fault shortens the crust and forms under compression.
items.correction_markdown: Normal fault: tension and extension. Reverse and thrust faults: compression and shortening.

items.erreur_markdown: "Any boundary between two beds is an unconformity."
items.pourquoi_faux: Between conformable beds deposition was continuous. An unconformity needs a gap in time, shown by erosion or non-deposition.
items.correction_markdown: Look for evidence of the gap: a basal conglomerate, a weathered or eroded surface, truncated structures, or a missing part of the fossil record.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) On a geological map the oldest rocks are in the centre of a fold, younger rocks lie outwards, and the beds dip away from the fold axis. Name the fold. (b) A vertical borehole meets the same coal seam twice, at $120\ \mathrm{m}$ and again at $215\ \mathrm{m}$ depth, with a fault between them. Is the fault normal or reverse, and which stress formed it? (c) State how a sinistral strike-slip fault differs from a dextral one.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) **Anticline**: oldest rocks in the core and limbs dipping away from the axis.

(b) A repeated bed means the hole has crossed the same seam twice, which happens at a **reverse fault**, formed by **compression**. (A normal fault would omit beds.)

(c) Looking across the fault, the opposite block appears to have moved to the left in a **sinistral** fault and to the right in a **dextral** fault.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) A limestone bed dips at $30^\circ$ and outcrops across level ground. The horizontal width of the outcrop, measured at right angles to the strike, is $80\ \mathrm{m}$. Calculate the true thickness of the bed and the thickness a vertical borehole would record. (b) A normal fault dips at $70^\circ$ and displaces a horizontal bed with a heave of $12\ \mathrm{m}$. Calculate the throw and the net slip.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) True thickness (perpendicular to the bedding) $= w\sin\delta = 80\sin 30^\circ = $ **$40.0\ \mathrm{m}$**. A vertical borehole records $w\tan\delta = 80\tan 30^\circ = $ **$46.2\ \mathrm{m}$** (check: $40.0/\cos 30^\circ = 46.2$).

(b) $\tan\delta = \text{throw}/\text{heave}$, so throw $= 12\tan 70^\circ = $ **$33.0\ \mathrm{m}$**. Net slip $= 12/\cos 70^\circ = $ **$35.1\ \mathrm{m}$** (check: $\sqrt{33.0^2 + 12^2} = 35.1$).

items.enonce_markdown: In a quarry face, granite is overlain by sandstone whose lowest layer contains pebbles of granite. The sandstone beds dip at $15^\circ$. Above them lie horizontal limestone beds with a weathered layer at the junction. A dolerite dyke cuts the granite and the sandstone but stops at the base of the limestone. A normal fault displaces the limestone, the sandstone, the granite and the dyke. (a) Name the junction between granite and sandstone, and the junction between sandstone and limestone. (b) Give the order of the five events or rocks from oldest to youngest. (c) State how many periods of erosion are recorded and give the evidence.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Granite to sandstone: **nonconformity** (sedimentary rock on eroded igneous rock). Sandstone to limestone: **angular unconformity** (tilted beds below, horizontal beds above).

(b) **Granite, sandstone, dolerite dyke, limestone, normal fault.** The pebbles of granite show that the granite was already formed and exposed; the dyke cuts granite and sandstone but not the limestone, so it is younger than the sandstone and older than the limestone; the fault cuts everything, so it is youngest.

(c) **At least two**: one between the granite and the sandstone (granite pebbles in a basal layer) and one between the sandstone and the limestone (the tilted sandstone is truncated, and a weathered layer lies at the junction).

items_markdown: An anticline has the oldest beds in its core and a syncline the youngest; use the ages on a map, not the shape of the land.
Hanging wall and footwall are positions; a normal fault has its hanging wall moved down (tension), a reverse or thrust fault has it moved up (compression).
Throw is vertical and heave is horizontal; for a horizontal bed $\tan\delta = \text{throw}/\text{heave}$ and net slip $= \text{throw}/\sin\delta$.
Classify faults by dip (thrust below about $45^\circ$), by relative movement (normal, reverse, strike-slip, oblique-slip) and by stress.
An unconformity marks a gap in time; angular, disconformity and nonconformity are told apart by what lies below and how the bedding compares.
Cross-cutting relationships give the order of events: a fault or intrusion is younger than what it cuts and older than what lies across it undisturbed.
